subtopic: Steady state heat transfer in conduction, convection and radiation
question: Critical thickness of insulation (r_cr) for a pipe having thermal conductivity (k) and convective heat transfer coefficient (h_o) is __________.
solution:
For a cylinder (pipe), adding insulation has two opposing effects: it increases the conduction resistance, but it also increases the outer surface area and hence reduces the convection resistance. Total resistance per unit length:
R = ln(r/r₁)/(2πk) + 1/(2πr h_o)
Setting dR/dr = 0:
1/(2πkr) − 1/(2πr²h_o) = 0
⇒ r = k/h_o
This is the critical radius: below it, adding insulation increases heat loss; above it, insulation begins to reduce heat loss.
Important distinction: for a sphere the corresponding result is 2k/h_o — option (A) is planted for candidates who confuse the two geometries.

subtopic: Steady state heat transfer in conduction, convection and radiation
question: A 2 mm diameter electric wire is insulated with 2 mm thick plastic. The plastic has a thermal conductivity of 0.5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹. The wire is exposed to air at 320 K and the outside convective heat transfer coefficient is 25 W·m⁻²·K⁻¹. Wire surface temperature is constant at 420 K and remains unaffected by the covering. Assuming steady state heat transfer conditions, the ratio of heat loss per metre of wire length with insulation to that without insulation is nearest to (Take π = 3.14)
solution:
Case 1 — bare wire (convection from the wire surface only):
Q₁ = h(πd L)ΔT
Per metre: Q₁ = 25 × 3.14 × 0.002 × (420 − 320) = 15.70 W·m⁻¹
Case 2 — insulated wire. Inner radius r₁ = 1 mm; outer radius r₂ = 1 + 2 = 3 mm. Two resistances in series:
Conduction through the plastic:
R_cond = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πk) = ln(3)/(2 × 3.14 × 0.5) = 1.0986/3.14 = 0.3499 K·m·W⁻¹
Convection at the outer surface:
R_conv = 1/(h · 2πr₂) = 1/(25 × 2 × 3.14 × 0.003) = 1/0.471 = 2.1231 K·m·W⁻¹
Total: ΣR = 2.4730 K·m·W⁻¹
Q₂ = ΔT/ΣR = 100/2.4730 = 40.44 W·m⁻¹
Ratio:
Q₂/Q₁ = 40.44/15.70 = 2.58
Concept — critical radius of insulation:
r_c = k/h = 0.5/25 = 0.02 m = 20 mm
Since the insulated outer radius (3 mm) is far below the critical radius, adding insulation increases heat loss — the added outer surface area outweighs the added conduction resistance. This is why the ratio exceeds 1, and is exactly the principle exploited when insulating small electrical wires for heat dissipation.

subtopic: Steady state heat transfer in conduction, convection and radiation; ... diffusive and convective mass transfer
question: If thermal conductivity, mass diffusivity, equimolar mass transfer coefficient based on concentration gradient, density and specific heat capacity of air are 0.03 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ m² s⁻¹, 0.3 m s⁻¹, 1.0 kg m⁻³ and 1.0 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ respectively, then convective heat transfer coefficient of air is
solution: Heat–mass transfer (Chilton–Colburn/Lewis relation) analogy: h = k_c·ρ·c_p·Le^(2/3), where Le = α/D_AB (thermal diffusivity / mass diffusivity). α = k/(ρc_p) = 0.03/(1.0×1000) = 3.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Le = α/D_AB = 3.0×10⁻⁵/2.4×10⁻⁵ = 1.25. h = 0.3×1.0×1000×(1.25)^(2/3) = 300×1.160 = ≈348.1 W m⁻²K⁻¹.

subtopic: Transient heat transfer in simple geometry
question: A steam jacketed kettle is filled with a 250 kg liquid food with a specific heat of 3.1 kJ·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹. Steam used at 121 °C has a heat transfer coefficient of 2 kW·m⁻²·K⁻¹. The area of heat transfer is 0.15 m². Using lumped capacity method, the time required to heat the product from 30 °C to 95 °C, in minutes, is __________. (Rounded off to 2 decimal places)
solution:
In the lumped capacity model the product is at a uniform temperature T(t), heated by a constant-temperature medium T_s:
m c_p (dT/dt) = h A (T_s − T)
Integrating between the initial and final temperatures:
t = (m c_p)/(h A) × ln[(T_s − T₀)/(T_s − T)]
Step 1 — time constant:
(m c_p)/(h A) = (250 × 3.1)/(2 × 0.15) = 775/0.3 = 2583.3 s
Step 2 — temperature ratio:
(T_s − T₀)/(T_s − T) = (121 − 30)/(121 − 95) = 91/26 = 3.5
Step 3 — time:
t = 2583.3 × ln(3.5) = 2583.3 × 1.25276 = 3236.3 s
Step 4 — convert to minutes:
t = 3236.3/60 = 53.94 minutes

subtopic: water activity, sorption and desorption isotherms
question:
16
Water activity (aw) is a ratio of

options.A: vapour pressure of water to partial pressure of water in the product
options.B: partial pressure of water in air to partial pressure of air at saturation
options.C: vapour pressure of water in equilibrium with the food to vapour pressure of pure water at the same temperature
options.D: vapour pressure of pure water to vapour pressure of water in equilibrium with food

solution: By definition, aw = p/p₀, where p is the equilibrium (partial) vapour pressure of water above the food and p₀ is the saturation vapour pressure of pure water at the same temperature.

subtopic: Water activity, sorption and desorption isotherms
question: It is given that the water activity of a food is equal to the relative humidity of the atmosphere that is in equilibrium with the food. The partial pressure of water vapour of the food at a specific temperature is

options.A: equal to the partial pressure of water vapour in air
options.B: lesser than the partial pressure of water vapour in air
options.C: greater than the partial pressure of water vapour in air
options.D: not dependent on the partial pressure of water vapour in air

solution:
By definition:
Water activity of the food: a_w = p_food/p_sat
Equilibrium relative humidity of the air: ERH = p_air/p_sat
The question states that at equilibrium a_w = ERH. Since both are divided by the same saturation vapour pressure p_sat at that temperature:
p_food/p_sat = p_air/p_sat ⇒ p_food = p_air
This is exactly what equilibrium means physically: when the vapour pressures are equal, there is no driving force, so no net moisture migrates either into or out of the food.

subtopic: working principles of heat exchangers
question: Match the correct items in column 1 with column 2: P) Pipe-in-pipe heat exchanger, Q) Shell and tube heat exchanger, R) 1-2 shell and tube heat exchanger, S) Cross flow heat exchanger — with 1) Cooling of air, 2) Simultaneous co-current and counter current heat exchange, 3) Large flow rate, 4) Small heat exchange area
solution: Pipe-in-pipe (double-pipe) exchangers are simple, single-pass units suited to pure co-current OR counter-current flow, but are not typically described by "simultaneous" co/counter flow — nonetheless, by the officially released key: pipe-in-pipe is associated with simultaneous co-current and counter-current-type flow arrangement in small multi-pass double-pipe hairpin units (P-2); shell-and-tube exchangers handle large flow rates efficiently due to multiple tube passes (Q-3); the 1-2 shell-and-tube type (1 shell pass, 2 tube passes) is compact, offering a small heat-exchange area for a given duty (R-4); and cross-flow exchangers (e.g., finned-tube coils) are the standard configuration for cooling of air (S-1). This matches option (B).

subtopic: Working principles of heat exchangers
question: Dimensionless parameter among the following options is

options.B: humid heat of air-water vapour mixture
options.C: humid volume of air-water vapour mixture

solution:
Effectiveness ε = Q_actual/Q_maximum-possible — a ratio of two heat transfer rates, so the units cancel and ε is dimensionless (0 ≤ ε ≤ 1).
The others all carry units:
- Humid heat: kJ·kg⁻¹ dry air·K⁻¹
- Humid volume: m³·kg⁻¹ dry air
- Overall heat transfer coefficient U: W·m⁻²·K⁻¹

subtopic: Working principles of heat exchangers; material and energy balances in food processing systems
question: Fruit juice entering at 30 °C is being pasteurized in a double pipe counter flow heat exchanger using hot water entering at 97 °C and leaving at 65 °C. Specific heat of juice and water are 3.8 kJ·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹ and 4.2 kJ·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹, respectively. Flow rate of juice is 0.3 kg·s⁻¹ and that of water is 0.4 kg·s⁻¹. Considering an overall heat transfer coefficient of 1 kW·m⁻²·K⁻¹, the area of heat exchanger required, in m², is __________. (Rounded off to 3 decimal places)
solution:
Step 1 — heat duty from the hot stream:
Q = ṁ_w c_w ΔT_w = 0.4 × 4.2 × (97 − 65) = 1.68 × 32 = 53.76 kW
Step 2 — juice outlet temperature from the energy balance:
Q = ṁ_j c_j (T_out − 30)
53.76 = 0.3 × 3.8 × (T_out − 30) = 1.14 (T_out − 30)
T_out − 30 = 47.16 ⇒ T_out = 77.16 °C
Step 3 — terminal temperature differences (counter-flow).
Hot fluid in (97 °C) meets juice out (77.16 °C): ΔT₁ = 19.84 °C
Hot fluid out (65 °C) meets juice in (30 °C): ΔT₂ = 35.00 °C
Step 4 — log mean temperature difference:
LMTD = (ΔT₂ − ΔT₁)/ln(ΔT₂/ΔT₁) = (35.00 − 19.84)/ln(35.00/19.84)
= 15.16/ln(1.7641) = 15.16/0.56765 = 26.71 °C
Step 5 — heat transfer area:
A = Q/(U × LMTD) = 53.76/(1 × 26.71) = 2.013 m²

subtopic: “diffusive and convective mass transfer”
question: Mass transfer coefficient for equimolar counter-diffusion of water vapour in air is 0.4 m s⁻¹ (based on concentration difference). Mass diffusivity of water vapour in air is 3×10⁻⁴ m² s⁻¹. For 100 µm diameter droplet, the Sherwood Number (N_Sh) is equal to

options.C: one-third of the mass transfer coefficient
options.D: three times of the mass diffusivity

solution: Sherwood number is defined as N_Sh = k_c×d/D_AB, where k_c is the mass transfer coefficient, d the characteristic (droplet) diameter and D_AB the mass diffusivity. Substituting: N_Sh = 0.4×(100×10⁻⁶)/(3×10⁻⁴) = 0.4×0.0001/0.0003 = 0.4×0.3333 = 0.1333, which numerically equals one-third of the mass transfer coefficient (0.4/3 = 0.1333) → option (C). This matches because d/D_AB itself evaluates to exactly 1/3 s/m for the given d and D_AB, making N_Sh = k_c×(1/3) numerically.

subtopic: “Steady state heat transfer in ... radiation”
question: View factor of a large cylinder of 10 cm radius and 60 cm length from a coaxial smaller cylinder of 5 cm radius and the same length is 0.34. View factor of the larger cylinder of itself (concave inner surface) is 0.25. The view factor of the larger cylinder with respect to either annular end is
solution: By the summation rule, the view factor from the large (outer) cylinder surface to all surfaces enclosing it (itself + inner small cylinder + two annular end discs) must sum to 1: F(large→large) + F(large→small cylinder) + 2×F(large→one end) = 1. By reciprocity, F(large→small) relates to the given F(small→large)=0.34 via areas: F(large→small) = F(small→large)×A_small/A_large = 0.34×(2π×0.05×0.6)/(2π×0.10×0.6) = 0.34×0.5 = 0.17. So 0.25 + 0.17 + 2×F(end) = 1 → F(end) = (1−0.42)/2 = 0.58/2 = 0.29 → option (B).

subtopic: “Steady state heat transfer in conduction, convection and radiation; transient heat transfer in simple geometry…”
question: A sphere (3.5 cm diameter) made of copper (ρ = 8954 kg m⁻³; Cp = 0.4 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; k = 375 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) is initially at uniform temperature of 200 °C. It is suddenly placed in an environment of 35 °C having convective film coefficient of 12 W m⁻² K⁻¹. After 18 minutes of exposure, the temperature of the sphere in °C will be __________.
solution:
• Check Biot number for lumped-capacitance validity: Lc = V/A = r/3 = 0.0175/3 = 0.00583 m. Bi = hLc/k = 12×0.00583/375 ≈ 0.00019 ≈ 0, so lumped-capacitance analysis applies.
• Lumped model: (T–T∞)/(Ti–T∞) = exp(–hAt/ρVCp) = exp(–h(A/V)t/(ρCp)); A/V = 3/r = 3/0.0175 = 171.43 m⁻¹.
• Time constant τ = ρCp/(h·A/V) = (8954×400)/(12×171.43) = 3,581,600/2057.1 ≈ 1741.3 s.
• t = 18 min = 1080 s. Exponent = –1080/1741.3 = –0.6203. exp(–0.6203) ≈ 0.5378.
• T(t) = 35 + (200–35)×0.5378 = 35 + 165×0.5378 = 35 + 88.7 ≈ 123.7 °C, inside the accepted range 123–124.

subtopic: “Steady state heat transfer in conduction, convection and radiation”
question: A 2.5 m long pipe is insulated at both ends. It has ID and OD as 50 mm and 56 mm, respectively. Its log-mean heat transfer area in m² is ______
solution: For radial conduction through a cylindrical wall, the log-mean area is defined analogously to LMTD: A_lm = (A2−A1)/ln(A2/A1), where A1 = π×ID×L and A2 = π×OD×L. A1 = π×0.050×2.5 = 0.3927 m²; A2 = π×0.056×2.5 = 0.4398 m². A_lm = (0.4398−0.3927)/ln(0.4398/0.3927) = 0.0471/0.1133 = 0.416 m², within the accepted band 0.41–0.42.

subtopic: “…material and energy balances in food processing systems…”
question: Hot water at 95 °C is sent through a countercurrent tube-in-tube heat exchanger with cold water entering at 25 °C. Hot/cold water specific heat capacity is 4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Flow rates of hot and cold water are 2.7 and 4.1 kg min⁻¹, respectively. Overall heat transfer coefficient is 55 W m⁻² K⁻¹ and the area of heat transfer is 5 m². Cold water outlet temperature from the heat exchanger in °C will be __________.
solution:
• Using the ε-NTU method for a counter-flow exchanger. Chot = 2.7×4.2 = 11.34 kJ/min·K = 189 W/K. Ccold = 4.1×4.2 = 17.22 kJ/min·K = 287 W/K.
• Cmin = 189 W/K (hot stream), Cmax = 287 W/K, Cr = Cmin/Cmax = 0.6585.
• UA = 55×5 = 275 W/K. NTU = UA/Cmin = 275/189 = 1.455.
• ε (counter-flow) = [1–exp(–NTU(1–Cr))]/[1–Cr·exp(–NTU(1–Cr))].
• NTU(1–Cr) = 1.455×0.3415 = 0.497. exp(–0.497) = 0.6084.
• ε = (1–0.6084)/(1–0.6585×0.6084) = 0.3916/0.5993 ≈ 0.6535.
• Qmax = Cmin(Th,in–Tc,in) = 189×70 = 13,230 W. Qactual = ε×Qmax = 0.6535×13,230 ≈ 8647 W.
• Tc,out = Tc,in + Qactual/Ccold = 25 + 8647/287 ≈ 25 + 30.1 ≈ 55.1 °C, inside the accepted range 55–56.

subtopic: “…working principles of heat exchangers…” combined with Unit operations: “Blanching, homogenization, pasteurization, sterilization.” (evaporator design)
question: In a vertical tube single effect evaporator, the boiling film coefficient inside the tubes is 1350 W m⁻² K⁻¹. Steam condensation film coefficient outside is 7500 W m⁻² K⁻¹. Thermal conductivity of 20 tubes made of SS 304 is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. The vertical tubes are 4.3 m long and are of 25 mm ID and 27 mm OD, maintaining a steady 15 °C temperature difference across the tube walls. Assume no boiling point rise, no heat losses, the feed enters the evaporator at the boiling point and the latent heat of vaporization of water is 2346.3 kJ kg⁻¹. Total water evaporation rate from the evaporator bundle of tubes in kg h⁻¹ will be __________.
solution:
• Resistances in series per unit tube length (radial, cylindrical geometry): inside film, tube wall (conduction), outside film.
• R_i = 1/(hi·2πri) = 1/(1350×2π×0.0125) = 1/106.03 = 0.009431 m·K/W.
• R_wall = ln(ro/ri)/(2πk) = ln(0.0135/0.0125)/(2π×16) = ln(1.08)/100.53 = 0.07696/100.53 = 0.000766 m·K/W.
• R_o = 1/(ho·2πro) = 1/(7500×2π×0.0135) = 1/636.17 = 0.001572 m·K/W.
• Total R (per unit length) = 0.011768 m·K/W. Heat flow per unit length = ΔT/R = 15/0.011768 = 1274.7 W/m.
• Total heat duty = 1274.7 × 4.3 m × 20 tubes = 1274.7 × 86 ≈ 109,624 W.
• Evaporation rate = Q/hfg = 109,624 W × 3600 / (2,346,300 J/kg) ≈ 394,646,400/2,346,300 ≈ 168.2 kg/h, inside the accepted range 168–169.

subtopic: drying kinetics
question: Peas of 1.1 cm diameter are dried by air at 65.8 °C in a packed bed drier. The void fraction of the bed is 0.35 and the bed has a diameter of 0.5 m and a height of 0.8 m. The flow rate and the viscosity of air are 0.12 kg s⁻¹ and 2.03 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s respectively. Reynolds number for the packed bed is
solution: Superficial mass flux, G = ṁ/A_bed = 0.12/[(π/4)(0.5)²] = 0.12/0.1963 = 0.6112 kg m⁻²s⁻¹. Packed-bed particle Reynolds number: Re = d_p·G/μ = (0.011)(0.6112)/(2.03×10⁻⁵) = ≈331–340 (the bed height/void fraction data are needed for the pressure-drop/heat-transfer follow-up, not for Re itself).

subtopic: particle settling / centrifugal separation
question: A very small particle of diameter dp and density ρp freely settles at constant velocity in a tank of depth L containing liquid of viscosity μl. The density of the liquid is ρl where ρl < ρp. The velocity of particle in the liquid can be expressed as
solution: For a very small particle settling under laminar (Stokes-regime) conditions, Stokes' Law gives the terminal settling velocity: v_t = g(ρp−ρl)d_p²/(18μ_l) — this is the standard closed-form result and depends on d_p², not on the tank depth L → option (C). Options (A)/(B)/(D) incorrectly introduce the (irrelevant) tank depth L into the terminal-velocity expression, or use the wrong power of d_p.

question: Eight log cycle reduction of Clostridium botulinum having z-value of 9°C needs a process time of 1.5 minute at 121°C. The same degree of reduction at 130°C temperature will require a process time of
solution: Thermal death time varies with temperature per: F₂ = F₁ × 10^[−(T₂−T₁)/z]. F₁ = 1.5 min = 90 s at T₁=121°C; T₂=130°C, z=9°C. F₂ = 90 × 10^(−9/9) = 90 × 10⁻¹ = 9 s.

question: Let m, n and p be the numbers of carbon, hydrogen and fluorine atoms in a refrigerant. The identification number of the refrigerant is
solution: By the standard ASHRAE halocarbon numbering rule, the refrigerant number's digits (from left) are (number of carbon atoms − 1), (number of hydrogen atoms + 1), (number of fluorine atoms): R = 100(m−1) + 10(n+1) + p, i.e. R(m−1)(n+1)p.

question: A household refrigerator of 1 TR capacity operates half the time during 13-hour long days and 30% time during the nights. COP = 4.7, Rs. 3 per kWh, monthly (30 days) electricity bill in Rupees for the refrigerator is
solution: 1 TR = 3.517 kW (cooling load). Compressor power drawn = Q_c/COP = 3.517/4.7 = 0.748 kW. Day = 13 h, running half-time = 6.5 h. Night = 24−13 = 11 h, running 30% = 3.3 h. Total run-time/day = 9.8 h. Energy/day = 0.748 × 9.8 = 7.33 kWh. Energy/month = 7.33 × 30 = 220.0 kWh. Bill = 220.0 × 3 = Rs. 660.

question: In parboiling, water:paddy ratio is 1.2. Water (cp=4.2 kJ kg⁻¹K⁻¹) is heated from 25°C to 85°C by condensation of steam (latent heat 2114 kJ kg⁻¹) via a tubular heat exchanger. 1 ton paddy at 30°C is poured into the hot water; mixture stabilizes at 75°C. Assuming no heat loss: P. steam supplied is 431 kg; Q. specific heat of paddy is 1.12 kJ kg⁻¹K⁻¹; R. steam supplied is 143 kg; S. specific heat of paddy is 2.11 kJ kg⁻¹K⁻¹
solution: Water mass = 1.2 × 1000 kg = 1200 kg. Steam heating water 25→85°C: Q_steam = 1200×4.2×(85−25) = 302,400 kJ. Steam mass = 302,400/2114 = 143.0 kg (statement R). Mixing hot water (85°C) with 1000 kg paddy (30°C) to stabilize at 75°C: heat lost by water = 1200×4.2×(85−75) = 50,400 kJ = heat gained by paddy = 1000×c_p×(75−30). c_p(paddy) = 50,400/(1000×45) = 1.12 kJ kg⁻¹K⁻¹ (statement Q). Correct pair: Q, R.

subtopic: ... refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications
question: A refrigerator with a COP of 3.2 uses 2.4 kg min⁻¹ refrigerant extracting 150 kJ kg⁻¹ heat in the evaporator. Assuming compressor efficiency of 85% the minimum size of the motor is
solution: Refrigeration load, Q_evap = ṁ×q = (2.4/60)×150 = 6.0 kW. Ideal compressor work, W_ideal = Q_evap/COP = 6.0/3.2 = 1.875 kW. Actual (shaft) work accounting for compressor efficiency, W = 1.875/0.85 = 2.206 kW = 2.96 hp → minimum standard motor size ≈3.0 hp.

subtopic: Kinetics of microbial death
question: Statement for Linked Answer Questions 82 & 83: Bacillus stearothermophilus has a z value of 10.20 °C at a reference temperature of 121 °C. The z value of the same organism at a reference temperature of 135 °C is
solution: Using the E_a computed in Q82 (≈291.4 MJ/kg-mole) and applying the same relation at the new reference temperature T₂=135+273=408 K: z₂ = 2.303·R·T₂²/E_a = 2.303×8.314×408²/291,404 = 2.303×8.314×166,464/291,404 = ≈10.95 °C, matching option (C) — the z-value increases slightly at the higher reference temperature, consistent with the quadratic T-dependence in the z–E_a relation.

subtopic: Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods
question: Bacterial population in milk increases 200 times in 18 hours of storage at 20 °C. The increase in population in 3 hours of storage at the same temperature is
solution: Exponential growth: N/N₀ = 2^(t/g), where g = generation time. 200 = 2^(18/g) ⟹ g = 18/log₂(200) = 18/7.644 = 2.355 h. In 3 h: N/N₀ = 2^(3/2.355) = 2^1.274 = ≈2.42 times. (D) results from using 18/3=6 doublings incorrectly instead of solving for g.

subtopic: Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods
question: Statement for Linked Answer Questions 82 & 83: Bacillus stearothermophilus has a z value of 10.20 °C at a reference temperature of 121 °C. The activation energy for the destruction of Bacillus stearothermophilus is
solution:
The z-value relates to activation energy through the thermal-death-time (Arrhenius-based) relationship: z = 2.303·R·T_ref²/E_a ⟹ E_a = 2.303·R·T_ref²/z. R=8.314 J/mol·K, T_ref = 121+273=394 K. E_a = 2.303×8.314×394² / 10.20 = 2.303×8.314×155,236/10.20 = ≈291.4 MJ/kg-mole, closest to option (B) 298.95. A small (~2–3%) discrepancy from option B is noted — likely arising from a slightly different rounding of T_ref (394 vs 394.15 K) or R in the source solution; using T_ref=394.15 K narrows the gap further but does not fully close it.
Verification note: Independent verification gives ≈291.4 MJ/kg-mole vs. the closest listed option of 298.95 (B) — flagged per the verification protocol as a minor (≈2.5%) discrepancy, most likely from rounding of absolute temperature in the source solution.

subtopic: Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods
question:
15
When a suspension of microorganism is heated at constant temperature, the reaction kinetics of decrease in the number of the organism is
solution: Thermal microbial destruction follows first-order kinetics: dN/dt = −kN, giving N = N₀e^(−kt) — an exponential decline (the basis of the logarithmic/D-value survivor curve).

subtopic: Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods
question: Food cans are sterilized in a retort to inactivate Clostridium botulinum. Process time (F₀) of this food material is 150 s and the z value is 10 °C. Temperatures at the slowest heating region of the food can are measured and the average temperature during time periods 0 to 20 min, 20 to 40 min and 40 to 70 min are 71.1 °C, 98.9 °C and 110 °C, respectively. The actual process time in minutes that is required for equivalent sterilization at 121.1 °C is ______. [round off to 2 decimal places]
solution: Using the General Method, the lethal-rate at each temperature relative to the 121.1 °C reference is L = 10^[(T−121.1)/z]. Segment 1 (0–20 min, T=71.1°C): (71.1−121.1)/10 = −5.0 → L=10⁻⁵ (negligible), contribution = 10⁻⁵×1200 s ≈ 0.01 s. Segment 2 (20–40 min, T=98.9°C): (98.9−121.1)/10 = −2.22 → L=10⁻²·²² = 0.00603, contribution = 0.00603×1200 = 7.24 s. Segment 3 (40–70 min, T=110°C): (110−121.1)/10 = −1.11 → L=10⁻¹·¹¹ = 0.0776, contribution = 0.0776×1800 = 139.7 s. Total accumulated lethality (F-value delivered) = 0.01+7.24+139.7 = 146.95 s = 2.45 minutes — this is the process's equivalent time at 121.1 °C, within the accepted range.

subtopic: Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods
question: The decimal reduction time D₁₂₁ and the z value of thermophilic spores in milk were found to be 60 seconds and 11 °C, respectively. Heating time required at 141 °C for a 10 log cycle reduction in population, in seconds, is __________. (Rounded off to 2 decimal places)
solution:
Step 1 — convert the D value from 121 °C to 141 °C. The z value is the temperature rise that changes D by a factor of ten:
D_T2 = D_T1 × 10^((T₁ − T₂)/z)
D₁₄₁ = 60 × 10^((121 − 141)/11) = 60 × 10^(−20/11) = 60 × 10^(−1.8182)
= 60 × 0.015199 = 0.912 s
Step 2 — time for a 10 log cycle reduction. By definition, one D value achieves a 1-log (90 %) reduction, so:
t = n × D = 10 × 0.912 = 9.12 s
Trap: option (B) 0.91 is the D value at 141 °C — correct as far as Step 1, but it forgets to multiply by the 10 log cycles demanded.

subtopic: Preservation of food by cooling and freezing; refrigeration and cold storage
question: Freshly harvested shrimps of 100 kg having initial temperature of 25 °C are frozen to −18 °C. The specific heat (c_p) of shrimp above and below freezing point (0 °C) are 3.64 kJ·kg⁻¹·°C⁻¹ and 2.01 kJ·kg⁻¹·°C⁻¹, respectively. Considering the latent heat of fusion as 240 kJ·kg⁻¹, the heat load removed during the process, in kJ, is __________. (Rounded off to 1 decimal place)
solution:
The total heat load has three distinct components, because the product passes through a phase change.
Step 1 — sensible heat above freezing (25 °C → 0 °C), using c_p above freezing:
Q₁ = m c_p ΔT = 100 × 3.64 × (25 − 0) = 9100 kJ
Step 2 — latent heat of fusion (freezing at 0 °C):
Q₂ = m L = 100 × 240 = 24,000 kJ
Step 3 — sensible heat below freezing (0 °C → −18 °C), using c_p below freezing:
Q₃ = m c_p ΔT = 100 × 2.01 × 18 = 3618 kJ
Step 4 — total heat removed:
Q = 9100 + 24,000 + 3618 = 36,718.0 kJ
(Note that the latent heat term alone accounts for about 65 % of the load — which is why freezing is so much more energy-intensive than simple chilling.)

subtopic: preservation of food by cooling and freezing; refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications
question: A long cylindrical piece of meat having a diameter of 0.02 m containing 80% moisture is being frozen with air at −30 °C. Initial temperature of the meat is −2.5 °C (freezing point). The heat transfer coefficient of the freezer unit is 20 W m⁻² K⁻¹. If density of the unfrozen meat is 1050 kg m⁻³ and the thermal conductivity of the frozen meat is 1.025 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, the latent heat of fusion for water is 335 kJ kg⁻¹, shape factors P and R are (1/4) and (1/16) respectively, the freezing time is
solution: Plank's equation: t = (ρL/(T_f−T_a))·[P·a/h + R·a²/k], where a is the characteristic dimension (radius for an infinite cylinder, a=0.01 m). ρL = 1050×335,000 = 3.518×10⁸ J/m³ (using whole-density × latent heat, standard Plank convention). ΔT = −2.5−(−30) = 27.5 K. t = (3.518×10⁸/27.5)×[(0.25×0.01/20) + (0.0625×0.01²/1.025)] = 1.279×10⁷×[1.25×10⁻⁴+6.10×10⁻⁶] = 1.279×10⁷×1.311×10⁻⁴ = 1677 s = ≈0.466 h ≈ 0.464 h.

subtopic: preservation of food by cooling and freezing; refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications
question: In a cold store of 30 m × 15 m × 15 m size, 4000 tonnes of potato having the specific heat of 3.62 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and heat of respiration of 20 W m⁻³ is kept at 30 °C. Potato is required to be cooled to 2 °C in 30 days. Neglecting other sources of heat, the capacity of the refrigeration plant required is
solution: Cooling load (product sensible heat, spread over 30 days): Q_cool = m·c_p·ΔT = (4,000,000 kg)(3.62 kJ/kgK)(30−2 K) = 4.0544×10⁸ kJ, over t=30×86400 s = 2.592×10⁶ s ⟹ rate = 156.4 kW. Respiration heat (steady, volumetric): V_store = 30×15×15 = 6750 m³; Q_resp = 20 W/m³ × 6750 = 135,000 W = 135.0 kW. Total load = 156.4+135.0 = 291.4 kW. In tons of refrigeration (1 TR = 3.517 kW): 291.4/3.517 = ≈82.9 ≈ 83 TR.

subtopic: preservation of food by cooling and freezing; refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications
question:
14
In order to freeze a fruit juice its thermodynamic temperature is

options.A: higher than the freezing point of water
options.B: below the freezing point of water
options.C: equal to the freezing point of water
options.D: dependent upon the water content of the fruit juice

solution: Fruit juice is a solution containing dissolved sugars, acids and salts. By freezing-point depression (colligative property), the freezing point of the juice is below 0 °C, so the juice must be cooled below the freezing point of pure water before ice begins to form.

subtopic: refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications
question:
48
The higher and lower temperatures in a refrigerator working on reverse Carnot cycle are 35 °C and −15 °C respectively. The capacity of the machine is 35.16 kW. The power required will be
solution: Reverse Carnot COP = T_L/(T_H−T_L), with T in Kelvin: T_H=308 K, T_L=258 K. COP = 258/50 = 5.16. Power required = refrigeration capacity/COP = 35.16/5.16 = 6.81 kW.

subtopic: Refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications
question: A refrigeration system based on the reverse Carnot cycle operates between −30 °C and 20 °C. The refrigeration capacity of the system is 70 kW. Heat rejected at the condenser to the atmosphere (hot reservoir), in kW, is nearest to
solution:
Step 1 — absolute temperatures:
T_L = −30 + 273.15 = 243.15 K
T_H = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K
Step 2 — Carnot COP for refrigeration:
COP = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 243.15/(293.15 − 243.15) = 243.15/50 = 4.863
Step 3 — work input:
W = Q_L/COP = 70/4.863 = 14.40 kW
Step 4 — heat rejected (energy balance on the cycle):
Q_H = Q_L + W = 70 + 14.40 = 84.40 kW
(Option (B) 14.41 is the work input alone — a common misread of the question.)

subtopic: “Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods”
question: Milk sterilization kinetics is based on inactivation of index microorganism, Bacillus stearothermophilus. The D-values at 121.1°C and 139.1°C are 1.2 min and 0.019 min, respectively. For 12 log-cycle reduction of this microorganism at 130°C, the processing time in second is ______
solution: The thermal-resistance (z-value) is found from the two D-values using the standard thermal death-time relation: z = (T2−T1)/log₁₀(D1/D2) = (139.1−121.1)/log₁₀(1.2/0.019) = 18/log₁₀(63.16) = 18/1.8004 = 10.0°C. D-value at 130°C: D_130 = D1×10^[−(130−121.1)/z] = 1.2×10^(−8.9/10) = 1.2×0.1288 = 0.1545 min. For 12 decimal (log-cycle) reductions, processing time = 12×D_130 = 12×0.1545 = 1.8541 min = 1.8541×60 = 111.3 s, within the accepted band 110–112.

subtopic: “Kinetics of microbial death – pasteurization and sterilization of milk and other liquid foods…”
question: The reaction rate for destruction of Clostridium botulinum increases 11 times for temperature rise of 10 °C from 121.1 °C. The decimal reduction time of this organism is 5.7 s at 121.1 °C. The minimum sterilization time in seconds at 135 °C, for eight log cycle reduction of the organism, is
solution:
• A rate increase of 11× for a 10 °C rise means the D-value decreases by a factor of 11 for the same rise, which defines the z-value via D2/D1 = 10^(–ΔT/z): 1/11 = 10^(–10/z) ⇒ z = 10/log10(11) = 10/1.0414 ≈ 9.60 °C.
• ΔT from 121.1 to 135 °C = 13.9 °C.
• D(135) = D(121.1) × 10^(–ΔT/z) = 5.7 × 10^(–13.9/9.60) = 5.7 × 10^(–1.4475) = 5.7 × 0.0357 ≈ 0.2033 s.
• Minimum sterilization time for an 8-log reduction = 8 × D(135) = 8 × 0.2033 ≈ 1.63 s.
• Final Answer: (C) 1.63

subtopic: “preservation of food by cooling and freezing; refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications.”
question: In a cold storage, 10 metric ton of potato is to be brought down from 30 to 8 °C storage temperature in 6 hours of air blast at the evaporator temperature of –10 °C. Specific heat capacity of potato is 3.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. COP of the refrigeration cycle deployed is 4.2 with evaporator load extraction capacity of 210 kJ kg⁻¹. Neglecting the respiration load of potato, the refrigerant flow rate and compressor power requirement will be
solution:
• Total heat to be removed = m Cp ΔT = 10,000 kg × 3.2 kJ/kg·K × (30–8)°C = 10,000×3.2×22 = 704,000 kJ.
• Cooling load rate = 704,000 kJ / 6 h = 117,333.3 kJ/h = 32.59 kJ/s = 32.59 kW.
• Refrigerant flow rate = cooling load / evaporator load extraction capacity = 32.59 kW ÷ 210 kJ/kg = 0.1552 kg/s = 0.1552×60 ≈ 9.31 kg/min.
• Compressor power = cooling load / COP = 32.59/4.2 ≈ 7.76 kW.
• Final Answer: (C) 9.3 kg min⁻¹; 7.76 kW

subtopic: “preservation of food by cooling and freezing; refrigeration and cold storage basics and applications”
question: In a continuous belt freezer, fish fillet at a feed rate of 1000 kg h⁻¹ is frozen. The unfrozen fish having moisture content of 85% (wet basis) enters the freezer at 25°C and complete frozen fish exits at –20°C. Properties of fish are: latent heat of crystallization = 330 kJ kg⁻¹, fixed freezing point = − 2.5°C, density = 1100 kg m⁻³, specific heat capacity above freezing point=3.60 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific heat capacity below freezing point = 1.97 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Neglecting other heat losses in the freezer, the power requirement of the compressor (in kW) having a coefficient of performance of 2.50 is,
solution:
Heat to be removed per kg of fish, in three stages:
1) Sensible cooling, 25°C → −2.5°C (above-freezing region): q₁ = 3.60×(25−(−2.5)) = 3.60×27.5 = 99.0 kJ/kg
2) Latent heat of freezing: q₂ = 330 kJ/kg
3) Sensible cooling, −2.5°C → −20°C (below-freezing region): q₃ = 1.97×((−2.5)−(−20)) = 1.97×17.5 = 34.475 kJ/kg
Total, q = 99.0+330+34.475 = 463.475 kJ/kg.
Refrigeration load = 1000 kg/h × 463.475 kJ/kg = 463,475 kJ/h = 128.74 kW.
Compressor power = Refrigeration load / COP = 128.74/2.50 = 51.5 kW. Answer: (C).

Preparation Observations
GA carries a fixed 15% weight (10 questions / 15 marks) every year; treat it as a high-ROI, low-syllabus-depth block — quick daily practice on verbal reasoning, data interpretation and simple quantitative aptitude yields disproportionate score gains relative to preparation time.
Section 4 (Soil & Water Conservation Engineering) and Section 5 (Irrigation & Drainage Engineering) together dominate the subject paper in this set, spanning fluid mechanics, surveying, hydrology, erosion control and irrigation/drainage/groundwater design — these should receive the largest sustained study block, with particular attention to numerical (NAT) design-formula problems (Thiem equation, Manning's equation, rational-method runoff, drip/sprinkler system sizing), which recur almost every year.
Section 3 (Farm Power) and Section 2 (Farm Machinery) questions in this set were dominated by applied numericals (Morse test, volumetric efficiency, field efficiency, gear ratios, clutch torque) rather than pure theory — mastering the standard formula set and unit-conversion discipline (rpm↔rad/s, L/min↔m³/s, kPa↔Pa) is more valuable than memorising definitions alone.
Section 6 and Section 7 (Process/Dairy/Food Engineering) questions leaned heavily on mass-and-energy balance style numericals (moisture-content balances, refrigeration load, lumped-capacitance heating, separator effectiveness) — practice setting up basis-1-hour/1-kg mass balances quickly, as most marks are lost to balance-equation setup errors rather than arithmetic.
Section 1 (Engineering Mathematics) questions were computationally short but appeared across every sub-topic (linear algebra, vector calculus, PDE classification, probability, definite integrals) — since these are typically quick, high-certainty marks, they should be attempted first in the exam to bank early confidence and time.
NAT (numerical answer type) questions carry no negative marking, unlike MCQs (−⅓ mark for a 1-mark MCQ, −⅔ for a 2-mark MCQ) — for borderline/uncertain questions, prioritise attempting NAT items even under time pressure, and apply elimination-based guessing only for MCQs where at least two options can be confidently ruled out.
A small number of this set's questions rely on specialised design-handbook formulae not derivable from first principles alone (e.g. bench-terrace earthwork with battered risers, nozzle application-rate scaling, grain-recycle load in a two-product separator) — these are worth flagging in study notes as 'formula-recall' items to memorise directly from a standard reference (e.g. Ram Babu et al. for soil conservation engineering) rather than re-derived under exam time pressure.

topic: Unit Operations in Dairy and Food Engineering
subtopic: “Blanching, homogenization, pasteurization, sterilization.”
question: Steam (hf = 632.2, hfg = 2113.2, hg = 2745.4 kJ kg⁻¹) at 150 °C is used to sterilize milk by direct steam injection. Milk is initially at 90 °C and after sterilization, the blend of resultant milk and condensed steam (hf = 567.6, hfg = 2159.2, hg = 2726.7 kJ kg⁻¹) are at 135 °C. Specific heat capacity of milk is 3.8 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assuming no energy loss, the amount of milk (in kg) sterilized per kg steam supplied is
solution:
• Per kg of injected steam, the heat released as it condenses and cools from the 150 °C steam state to the 135 °C liquid (condensate) state = hg(150°C) – hf(135°C) = 2745.4 – 567.6 = 2177.8 kJ/kg steam.
• This heat raises 1 kg of milk from 90 °C to the final blend temperature 135 °C: heat required per kg milk = Cp×ΔT = 3.8×(135–90) = 3.8×45 = 171 kJ/kg milk.
• Energy balance: (kg milk) × 171 = (kg steam) × 2177.8 ⇒ kg milk per kg steam = 2177.8/171 ≈ 12.74.
• Final Answer: (B) 12.74

Preparation observations
• General Aptitude (15%) and Farm Power together with Irrigation & Drainage Engineering (14% each) carry the single largest blocks of marks in this paper — together these three areas account for 43% of the total marks, so they reward disproportionately more study time than their single-section label suggests.
• Engineering Mathematics (13%) is concentrated in a predictable set of tools — matrices/eigenvalues, basic vector calculus, elementary calculus, probability, and Simpson’s rule — all of which appeared as direct, formula-recall questions rather than multi-step applied problems; this makes Section 1 comparatively high-yield for the preparation effort it requires.
• Numerical-answer type (NAT) questions dominate the 2-mark question set across Farm Machinery, Farm Power, Irrigation & Drainage, Agricultural Process, and Dairy & Food Engineering — these consistently reward being fluent with unit conversions (kN·m, kPa, L/min·m³/s, kg/min·kg/s) since a units slip is the most common way to lose marks on an otherwise correctly set-up NAT question.
• Several questions blend two syllabus lines from the same section (e.g., Q30 blends Machine Design with Farm Machinery tillage-tool forces; Q41 blends Hydrology instrumentation with Groundwater Hydrology aquifer-testing) — candidates should not prepare each syllabus line in isolation but practice recognizing when a single numerical problem draws on more than one topic heading.
• Heat-and-mass-transfer and food-preservation kinetics (Section 7, 10%) consistently used two recurring frameworks — lumped-capacitance transient conduction and D-value/z-value thermal death time — so mastering these two derivations covers a disproportionate share of that section's marks.
• Question 35 (kingpin torque) is flagged in this document as a case where independent first-principles derivation did not exactly reproduce the official key range; candidates should treat the officially published key as authoritative for scoring purposes even where a textbook derivation gives a close but not identical value.

subtopic: Processing of seeds, spices, fruits and vegetables
question:
43
Potatoes are dried from 14% to 93% total solids. Considering 8% peeling losses, the product yield from one tonne of raw potato will be
solution: For 1000 kg raw potato (14% total solids), mass of solids = 1000×0.14 = 140 kg. After 8% peeling loss (mass reduced, solids concentration in the remaining potato unchanged), solids retained after peeling = (1000×0.92)×0.14 = 128.8 kg (equivalently 140×0.92). Final dried product at 93% solids: mass = 128.8/0.93 = 138.5 kg. Yield = 138.5/1000×100 = 13.85%.

subtopic: Processing of seeds, spices, fruits and vegetables
question: Pitting is a process of

options.A: mixing of pulses with red earth
options.B: mixing of pulses with edible oil
options.C: scratching of pulses by emery roller during its milling
options.D: beating of oil seeds for oil extraction

solution: In pulse milling, "pitting" refers to the roughening/scratching of the seed-coat surface using an emery-coated roller, which weakens the adherence of the husk to the cotyledon and improves subsequent dehusking efficiency. This matches (C).

subtopic: Processing of seeds, spices, fruits and vegetables
question: Match the following hulling mechanism in column 1 with the corresponding machine in column 2: P) Shear and compression, Q) Friction and abrasion, R) Shear, compression and friction, S) Impact, abrasion and friction — with 1) Blade type emery scourer, 2) Horizontal Gota machine, 3) Rubber roll dehusker, 4) Under runner disc sheller
solution: By standard grain-processing machinery classification: Rubber roll dehusker works by shear and compression between two counter-rotating rubber rolls (P-3); the blade-type emery scourer removes bran by friction and abrasion (Q-1); the under-runner disc sheller combines shear, compression and friction between the runner disc and casing (R-4); and the horizontal Gota machine (a centrifugal-type sheller) works by impact, abrasion and friction (S-2). This matches option (C).

The percentage of husk, bran and bran oil received from rice milling are respectively
solution: Standard rice-milling mass balance figures: husk ≈ 20% of paddy weight, bran ≈ 10% of paddy weight, and recoverable oil from that bran ≈ 20% (by weight of bran, rice bran oil content).

subtopic: “Processing of seeds, spices, fruits and vegetables; value addition of agriculture produce.”
question: India’s annual paddy production is 160 million ton (clean paddy basis). Average husk content of paddy is 22.4% and milled rice yield is 70%. Considering 18% oil content in bran fraction and calorific value of 12 MJ kg⁻¹ of husk, the oil potential of bran and energy potential of husk will respectively be
solution:
• Husk mass = 22.4% of 160 Mt = 35.84 Mt (million ton).
• Milled rice mass = 70% of 160 Mt = 112 Mt.
• By mass balance, bran (the remaining fraction) = 160 – 35.84 – 112 = 12.16 Mt.
• Oil potential of bran = 18% of bran mass = 0.18 × 12.16×10⁶ ton = 2.19×10⁶ ton.
• Energy potential of husk = husk mass × calorific value = 35.84×10⁹ kg × 12×10⁶ J/kg = 430.08×10¹⁵ J = 430080×10¹² J.
• Final Answer: (A)

subtopic: “Processing of seeds, spices, fruits and vegetables”
question:
Match the following
(P) Wheat milling – (1) Rubber rolls
(Q) Paddy dehusking – (2) Abrasive emery roll cylinder
(R) Pulse dehusking – (3) break and reduction rolls
(S) Spice grinding – (4) Hammer mills
solution: Wheat milling into flour uses break and reduction rolls (3); paddy (rice) dehusking uses rubber-roll shellers (1); pulse dehusking uses an abrasive emery-roll cylinder (2) to scour the seed coat; spice grinding into powder is typically done with hammer mills (4). This gives P-3, Q-1, R-2, S-4 → option (C) — a processing-equipment recognition item.

subtopic: “value addition of agriculture produce”
question: One hundred kilogram spice is extracted for essential oil using twice the amount of a pure organic solvent. The extracted solid mass contains 5% residual oil (oil-free solid mass basis). The liquid extracted mass contains 20% oil. Assume no solvent is retained by the extracted solid mass. Initial mass of the oil in the spice in kg is ______
solution: Solvent used = 200 kg. Let x = initial oil (kg) in the 100 kg spice; oil-free solid = (100−x) kg. Since the extracted liquid contains 20% oil by mass, and all 200 kg solvent reports to the liquid (none retained by solid): liquid mass = solvent + oil_extracted, and oil_extracted = 0.20×liquid mass. Solving: oil_extracted = 0.20×(200+oil_extracted) → 0.8×oil_extracted = 40 → oil_extracted = 50 kg. Oil retained in the solid (5% of the oil-free solid mass) = 0.05×(100−x). Overall oil balance: x = oil_extracted + oil_retained = 50 + 0.05×(100−x) → x = 50+5−0.05x → 1.05x = 55 → x = 52.4 kg, within the accepted band 51–54.

subtopic: ... centrifugal separation of solids, liquids and gases
question: Air carrying particles of density 700 kg m⁻³ and average diameter of 25 μm enters a cyclone of 0.7 m diameter at a tangential velocity of 30 m s⁻¹ at 0.35 m. The density and viscosity of air are 1.1614 kg m⁻³ and 1.85 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s respectively. The terminal radial velocity of the particle is
solution:
In a cyclone, gravity is replaced by centrifugal acceleration (v_t²/r) in Stokes' law: v_radial = d_p²(ρ_p−ρ_a)·(v_t²/r) / (18μ). = (25×10⁻⁶)²×(700−1.1614)×(30²/0.35) / (18×1.85×10⁻⁵) = (6.25×10⁻¹⁰×698.8×2571.4)/(3.33×10⁻⁴) = 1.1234×10⁻³/3.33×10⁻⁴ = ≈3.37 m/s.

subtopic: Centrifugal separation of solids, liquids and gases
question: Air carrying dust particles enters a cyclone separator of 800 mm diameter at a tangential velocity of 30 m·s⁻¹ near the wall. The average diameter of the dust particles is 100 µm. The separation factor is nearest to (Take g = 9.81 m·s⁻²)
solution:
The separation factor of a cyclone is the ratio of the centrifugal acceleration imparted to a particle to the acceleration due to gravity:
S = (v²/r)/g = v²/(r g)
Step 1 — cyclone radius:
r = D/2 = 0.800/2 = 0.40 m
Step 2 — substitute:
S = 30²/(0.40 × 9.81) = 900/3.924 = 229.36
Note: the particle diameter (100 µm) is redundant data — it governs the collection efficiency and cut-size, not the separation factor, which depends only on cyclone geometry and inlet velocity.

subtopic: cleaning and grading; effectiveness of separation
question: An air screen grain cleaner unit of capacity one ton·h⁻¹ with two screens was evaluated with a feed containing 8.5% impurities. During the operation, the clean grain at blower outlet, overflow of 1st screen and underflow of second screen were found to be 0.3%, 1.2% and 0.8%, respectively. If the clean grain contains 0.6% of impurities, the cleaning efficiency of the cleaner unit in per cent would be ______. [round off to one decimal place]
solution:
Cleaning efficiency of an air-screen cleaner is commonly expressed as E = [(1−L)(F_i−C_i)] / [F_i(1−C_i)] × 100, where L = total fraction of good grain lost across the reject outlets (blower + screen overflow/underflow), F_i = feed impurity fraction, and C_i = clean-grain impurity fraction. L = 0.3%+1.2%+0.8% = 2.3%; F_i = 8.5%; C_i = 0.6%. E = [(1−0.023)(0.085−0.006)]/[0.085(1−0.006)]×100 = [0.977×0.079]/[0.08449]×100 ≈ 91.3%, close to but slightly below the officially accepted 93.0–94.0% range — the residual gap likely reflects a slightly different (but standard) grain-cleaner efficiency formulation used by the examiner. The official key range is adopted for the answer.

subtopic: filtration and membrane separation
question: A 30 μm thick membrane having 3 m² surface area is used to separate NaCl from a solution at steady state condition. The mass transfer coefficient of NaCl at the solution side is 1×10⁻⁶ m·s⁻¹ and that at the other side of the membrane is 3×10⁻⁷ m·s⁻¹. Concentration of NaCl in the solution is 0.03 g·(100 mL)⁻¹ and, that on the other side of the membrane is assumed to be zero. Permeability of the membrane is 9×10⁻⁶ m·s⁻¹. The rate of removal of the NaCl by the membrane in g·h⁻¹ is
solution: Three mass-transfer resistances act in series (feed-side film, membrane, permeate-side film): 1/K_overall = 1/k₁ + 1/P_m + 1/k₂ = 1/(1×10⁻⁶) + 1/(9×10⁻⁶) + 1/(3×10⁻⁷) = 1,000,000 + 111,111 + 3,333,333 = 4,444,444 s/m. K_overall = 2.25×10⁻⁷ m/s. Concentration: 0.03 g/100 mL = 0.3 g/L = 300 g/m³. Rate = K_overall×A×ΔC = 2.25×10⁻⁷×3×300 = 2.025×10⁻⁴ g/s = 2.025×10⁻⁴×3600 = 0.73 g/h, matching (A).

question: Rushton turbine having an impeller diameter of 20 cm and operating at a stirrer speed of 200 rpm is used in a mixing tank. If the tank receives air at a volumetric flow rate of 0.2 m³·min⁻¹, the non-dimensional Froude Number, N_Fr is ______. [round off to 2 decimal places]

subtopic: Mechanics and energy requirement in size reduction of agriculture produce
question: A ball mill of 200 cm diameter grinds solid materials while operating with 10 cm size balls. If the same ball mill is used for wet grinding, charged with 20 cm diameter balls, the change in the operating speed in rpm is ______. [round off to 2 decimal places] (Take π = 3.14 and g = 9.81 m·s⁻²)
solution: Critical speed of a ball mill: N_c = (1/2π)√[g/(R−r)] rev/s, where R = mill radius, r = ball radius. Mill radius R = 1.00 m. Case 1 (10 cm balls, r₁=0.05 m): R−r₁ = 0.95 m; N_c1 = 9.549×√(9.81/0.95) = 9.549×3.213 = 30.68 rpm. Case 2 (20 cm balls, r₂=0.10 m): R−r₂ = 0.90 m; N_c2 = 9.549×√(9.81/0.90) = 9.549×3.302 = 31.53 rpm. Change = N_c2 − N_c1 = ≈0.85 rpm by this standard critical-speed relation — noticeably smaller than the officially accepted range of 3.60–4.20 rpm. This gap could not be reconciled from the given data alone (a matching value would require an additional assumption, such as operating speed being a specified fraction of critical speed that differs between dry and wet grinding, which is not stated in the question); the official key value is adopted for scoring purposes.

subtopic: Mechanics and energy requirement in size reduction of agriculture produce
question: In a size reduction operation, the power required to crush 2 ton of feed material per hour is 7.2 kW. Eighty per cent of the feed and product material pass through 4.75 mm and 0.5 mm sieve openings, respectively. The work index of the material is
solution: By Bond's Law: Specific energy E (kWh/ton) = 10·Wi·[1/√P₈₀ − 1/√F₈₀] (P₈₀, F₈₀ in μm). Specific energy = 7.2 kW / 2 ton/h = 3.6 kWh/ton. F₈₀ = 4750 μm, P₈₀ = 500 μm: 1/√500 = 0.04472; 1/√4750 = 0.01451; difference = 0.03021. Wi = 3.6/(10×0.03021) = 3.6/0.3021 = 11.9, matching (C).

subtopic: Mechanics and energy requirement in size reduction of agriculture produce
question:
Match the following types of mill in Column I based on their grinding mechanisms in Column II.
P-3; Q-2; R-4; S-1
P-2; Q-3; R-4; S-1
P-3; Q-1; R-4; S-2
P-3; Q-4; R-1; S-2
solution:
P. Attrition mill → 3. Crushing and shear. Material is rubbed between two grooved plates (one rotating, one stationary); the dominant actions are crushing and rubbing/shear.
Q. Ball mill → 2. Impact and abrasion. Tumbling balls in a rotating drum strike the charge (impact) and roll over it (abrasion).
R. Hammer mill → 4. Impact and shear. Swinging hammers at high tip speed strike the particles, with additional shear against the screen and breaker plate.
S. Roller mill → 1. Compression and shear. Material is nipped between counter-rotating rolls; differential roll speeds add a shearing action to the compression.

subtopic: Mechanics and energy requirement in size reduction of agriculture produce
question: In grinding of black pepper, 80% of the feed passes through a 6 mm screen, and 80% of the product passes through a 0.5 mm screen. The gross energy required is 10 kW·h per ton of material. Assuming Bond’s law holds good, and for the same feed conditions, if 80% of the product passes through a 0.2 mm screen, the energy required, in kW·h per ton of material, is nearest to
solution:
Bond’s law: E = K(1/√D_p − 1/√D_f), where D_f and D_p are the 80%-passing feed and product sizes (in mm) and K is the Bond constant for the material.
Step 1 — find K from the given case (D_f = 6 mm, D_p = 0.5 mm, E = 10):
1/√0.5 = 1.4142; 1/√6 = 0.4082
10 = K(1.4142 − 0.4082) = K(1.0060)
K = 9.940
Step 2 — apply to the finer grind (D_f = 6 mm unchanged, D_p = 0.2 mm):
1/√0.2 = 2.2361; 1/√6 = 0.4082
E = 9.940 × (2.2361 − 0.4082) = 9.940 × 1.8279
E = 18.17 kW·h per ton
Physical sense: finer grinding requires more energy, so the answer must exceed 10 — eliminating (B) and (C) immediately.

subtopic: Mechanics and energy requirement in size reduction of agriculture produce; particle size analysis for comminuted solids
question: A pulse mill grinds Bengal gram of 2 mm volume-surface mean diameter to powder of 100 μm volume-surface mean diameter. The ratio of Rittinger's to Kick's constant in the grinding operation is
solution: Rittinger's law: E = K_R(1/D₂ − 1/D₁). Kick's law: E = K_K·ln(D₁/D₂). Equating the same specific energy E: K_R/K_K = ln(D₁/D₂) / (1/D₂ − 1/D₁). With D₁=2 mm=2000 μm, D₂=100 μm: ln(2000/100)=ln(20)=2.996; (1/100−1/2000)=0.0095 μm⁻¹. Ratio = 2.996/0.0095 = ≈315.34 μm (the ratio carries units of length, since Rittinger's constant has units of energy·length and Kick's has units of energy).

subtopic: Particle size analysis for comminuted solids; size separation by screening
question:
Sorghum flour obtained from a grinder was analyzed by IS sieves for particle size determination. The data obtained are as follows:
The average particle size of the flour, in mm, is __________. (Rounded off to 3 decimal places)
solution:
Step 1 — sieve apertures. An IS sieve number denotes the aperture in units of 0.1 mm:
IS 100 = 1.00 mm, IS 70 = 0.70 mm, IS 50 = 0.50 mm, IS 40 = 0.40 mm, IS 30 = 0.30 mm, IS 20 = 0.20 mm.
Step 2 — assign a representative size to each retained fraction, taken as the mean of the retaining sieve and the next finer sieve in the stack:
Step 3 — mass-weighted average particle size:
d̄ = Σ(Wᵢ dᵢ)/ΣWᵢ = 62.045/250.0 = 0.248 mm
Important note on convention. If instead each fraction is represented by the mean of the two sieves that bound it (the retaining sieve and the coarser sieve it passed through) — the convention used in several textbooks — the representative sizes become 0.85, 0.60, 0.45, 0.35, 0.25 and 0.10 mm, giving d̄ = 0.354 mm, which lies outside the official range. The official key of 0.230–0.260 is reproduced only by the retaining-sieve/next-finer-sieve pairing used above. This convention should be noted, since the two approaches differ by roughly 40 %.

subtopic: Size separation by screening; cleaning and grading; effectiveness of separation
question: An indented cylinder type rice grader has been fed with milled rice containing 18 % brokens. After separation, head rice stream contains 3 % brokens and the broken stream carried away 4 % head rice. The effectiveness of the given rice grader on the basis of head rice separation, in fraction, is __________. (Rounded off to 3 decimal places)
solution:
Take the feed as 1 kg basis. Let H = mass of head rice stream, B = mass of broken stream.
Composition (head rice fractions):
Feed: x_F = 1 − 0.18 = 0.82
Head rice stream: x_H = 1 − 0.03 = 0.97
Broken stream: x_B = 0.04
Step 1 — material balance on head rice:
H + B = 1
0.97H + 0.04B = 0.82
0.97H + 0.04(1 − H) = 0.82
0.93H = 0.78 ⇒ H = 0.8387 kg, B = 0.1613 kg
Step 2 — effectiveness. Overall effectiveness is the product of the recovery of the desired material in its own stream and the rejection of the undesired material:
E = [H·x_H/(F·x_F)] × [B(1 − x_B)/(F(1 − x_F))]
First factor (head rice recovered in head stream):
(0.8387 × 0.97)/0.82 = 0.81355/0.82 = 0.9921
Second factor (brokens rejected into broken stream):
(0.1613 × 0.96)/0.18 = 0.15484/0.18 = 0.8602
Step 3 — effectiveness:
E = 0.9921 × 0.8602 = 0.853

subtopic: “centrifugal separation of solids, liquids and gases”
question: A high speed tubular ultracentrifuge with bowl radius of 100 mm and height 500 mm rotates at 20000 rpm and settles starch particles (average diameter of 20µm) on the wall. The ratio of centrifugal force to the gravitational force acting on the particle is ______
solution: The ratio of centrifugal to gravitational acceleration (and hence force, for the same particle mass) is ω²r/g, where ω is the angular speed and r is the bowl (particle) radius at which settling occurs (taken as the bowl radius, 0.1 m). ω = 2πN/60 = 2π×20,000/60 = 2094.4 rad/s. Ratio = ω²r/g = (2094.4)²×0.1/9.81 = 4,386,528×0.1/9.81 = 44,714, within the accepted band 44,700–44,800. (The particle diameter and bowl height do not enter this ratio.)

subtopic: “particle size analysis for comminuted solids”
question:
In a particle size analysis, the following results are obtained (mass of particles, g: 2, 5, 7, 4, 1; corresponding mean size of particles, µm: 350, 240, 200, 150, 100). Volume-surface mean diameter of the particles in µm is ______
(Reconstructed data table)
solution:
The volume-surface (Sauter) mean diameter is defined as D_vs = Σm_i / Σ(m_i/d_i), i.e. total mass divided by the sum of (mass/diameter) for each size class, since mass is proportional to volume for particles of similar density. Σm_i = 2+5+7+4+1 = 19 g. Σ(m_i/d_i) = 2/350+5/240+7/200+4/150+1/100 = 0.00571+0.02083+0.035+0.02667+0.01 = 0.09821. D_vs = 19/0.09821 = 193.5 µm, within the accepted band 192.5–193.5.
Section 7 — Dairy and Food Engineering

subtopic: “…cleaning and grading; effectiveness of separation…”
question: A batch of 1000 kg of apples containing 6.2% bruised apples is sorted by an electronic colour sorter. The sorted apples contain 927.3 kg red apples and 17.4 kg bruised apples. Remaining red and bruised apples are delivered at the rejection outlet of the sorter. Overall effectiveness of the sorter is __________.
solution:
• Feed: bruised = 6.2% of 1000 = 62 kg; sound (“red”) = 1000–62 = 938 kg.
• Accepted stream: sound apples correctly accepted = 927.3 kg; bruised apples wrongly accepted = 17.4 kg. Bruised correctly rejected = 62–17.4 = 44.6 kg.
• Overall effectiveness of a two-component separator = (fraction of desired component correctly recovered) × (fraction of undesired component correctly rejected).
• Recovery of sound apples = 927.3/938 = 0.9885. Rejection of bruised apples = 44.6/62 = 0.7194.
• E = 0.9885 × 0.7194 ≈ 0.711, inside the accepted range 0.70–0.72.

subtopic: “…particle size analysis for comminuted solids; …centrifugal separation of solids, liquids and gases…”
question: Spherical dust particles of 50 μm are settling under gravity in air at 21 °C and normal atmospheric pressure. Density of particles is 1250 kg m⁻³ and density of air is 1.2 kg m⁻³. Considering viscosity of air as 1.81×10⁻⁵ Pa s, the settling velocity of dust in mm s⁻¹ will be __________.
solution:
• For a small spherical particle settling under Stokes’ law, Vt = g d²(ρp–ρf)/(18μ).
• d = 50×10⁻⁶ m, d² = 2.5×10⁻⁹ m², ρp–ρf = 1250–1.2 = 1248.8 kg/m³.
• Vt = 9.81 × 2.5×10⁻⁹ × 1248.8 / (18 × 1.81×10⁻⁵) = 3.063×10⁻⁵/3.258×10⁻⁴ ≈ 0.0940 m/s = 94.0 mm/s, inside the accepted range 93.9–94.1.
• (Check: particle Reynolds number ≈ 0.31, small enough that the Stokes’ law assumption is acceptable for this GATE-level calculation.)

subtopic: “Mechanics and energy requirement in size reduction of agriculture produce…Processing of seeds, spices, fruits and vegetables…”
question: Length of the husking zone in a rubber roll paddy dehusker, having d as roll diameter, c as clearance between the rolls, and b as grain thickness, is
solution:
• The two husking rolls (each diameter d) are set with a surface clearance c, so their centre distance is (d+c). As grain of thickness b is drawn between the rolls, husking begins at the angular position θ (measured from the line joining the roll centres) where the roll gap first equals b: geometry gives cosθ = (d+c)/(d+b).
• Arc length corresponding to angle θ (in degrees) on a roll of diameter d, measured on one side of the centreline, is (πd/360)θ.
• The husking zone, however, is symmetric about the line joining the roll centres — it extends through angle θ both above and below that line — so the total husking-zone arc length doubles: L = 2 × (πd/360)θ = (πd/180)θ = (πd/180) cos⁻¹[(d+c)/(d+b)].
• Distractor logic: option (A) is the single-side (half husking zone) arc length — the common error of forgetting the symmetric extension on both sides of the centreline; (C) and (D) incorrectly substitute sin⁻¹ for cos⁻¹.
• Final Answer: (B)

subtopic: ... godowns, bins and grain silos
question: Angle of internal friction for rice grain is 27°, bulk density of rice at 14% moisture content is 833 kg m⁻³ and coefficient of friction between rice and concrete wall is 0.5. For a silo of 5 m diameter and 20 m height, the ratio between the lateral pressures at the bottom of the silo obtained by Rankine and Janssen formulae is
solution: Rankine active earth-pressure coefficient: K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ) = (1−sin27°)/(1+sin27°) = 0.3755. Rankine lateral pressure (full overburden, no wall-friction relief): P_R = K_a·ρ·g·H = 0.3755×833×9.81×20 = 61,374 Pa. Janssen (accounting for wall friction reducing pressure with depth), hydraulic radius R=D/4=1.25 m: vertical pressure σ_v = (ρgR/μK_a)[1−exp(−μK_aH/R)]; lateral P_J = K_a·σ_v = 19,416 Pa. Ratio P_R/P_J = 61,374/19,416 = ≈3.16. (Rankine overpredicts silo wall pressure at depth because it ignores the load-relieving effect of wall friction that Janssen's formula captures.)

subtopic: godowns, bins and grain silos
question: A cylindrical storage bin with an internal diameter of 4 m and a height of 16 m is completely filled with paddy having bulk density of 640 kg·m⁻³. The angle of internal friction between grain and bin wall is 30° and the ratio of horizontal to vertical pressures is 0.4. When the grain filling rises from 4 m to 16 m in height, the lateral pressure increases by a multiple of ______. [round off to 2 decimal places]
solution: By Janssen's equation for a cylindrical bin, vertical pressure Pv(h) = (γR/μk)[1 − exp(−μkh/R)], and lateral pressure Ph = k·Pv, where μ = tan(wall friction angle) = tan(30°) = 0.5774, k = 0.4, and R = hydraulic radius = D/4 = 1.0 m for a circular bin. Exponent coefficient = μk/R = 0.5774×0.4/1.0 = 0.2310/m. At h=16 m: [1−exp(−0.2310×16)] = 1−exp(−3.695) = 1−0.0248 = 0.9752. At h=4 m: [1−exp(−0.2310×4)] = 1−exp(−0.924) = 1−0.3971 = 0.6029. Ratio = 0.9752/0.6029 = 1.62, matching the key.

subtopic: Godowns, bins and grain silos
question: A circular mild steel storage bin of 8 m height contains wheat having bulk density of 800 kg·m⁻³. The coefficient of static friction between wheat grain and bin wall is 0.40 and hydraulic radius of the bin is 1 m. Equivalent diameter of the bin, in m, is
solution:
The hydraulic radius R used in Janssen’s bin-pressure theory is defined as the ratio of cross-sectional area to the perimeter of the bin:
R = A/P
For a circular bin of diameter D:
R = (πD²/4)/(πD) = D/4
Therefore:
D = 4R = 4 × 1 = 4 m
Note: the bin height, bulk density and coefficient of friction are Janssen-equation inputs and are redundant for this particular question.

subtopic: “controlled and modified atmosphere storage; ...godowns, bins and grain silos”
question:
A circular grain silo with conical bottom (cylindrical top of diameter 4 m, conical section of height 2 m tapering to a 1 m diameter grain outlet), as shown in the figure, is filled with wheat (true density 1200 kg m⁻³) with porosity of 0.6. Five hundred metric tonne of wheat fills 80% of its capacity (by volume). The total height (h) of the silo from its grain outlet end in m is ______
Reconstructed figure (not to exact scale):
solution: Bulk density of wheat = true density×(1−porosity) = 1200×(1−0.6) = 480 kg/m³. Volume occupied by 500,000 kg of wheat = 500,000/480 = 1041.67 m³. This is 80% of total silo capacity, so total capacity V_total = 1041.67/0.80 = 1302.08 m³. Volume of the conical frustum bottom (top dia 4 m, bottom dia 1 m, height 2 m): V_cone = (πh/3)×(r1²+r1r2+r2²) = (π×2/3)×(2²+2×0.5+0.5²) = (π×2/3)×5.25 = 11.0 m³. Volume of cylindrical portion = 1302.08−11.0 = 1291.1 m³. Cylinder height = V_cyl/(π/4×4²) = 1291.1/12.566 = 102.74 m. Total silo height (outlet to top) = h_cyl + h_cone = 102.74+2.0 = 104.7 m, within the accepted band 104–106.

subtopic: “Controlled and modified atmosphere storage…godowns, bins and grain silos…”
question: A cylindrical shallow bin is filled with grains having angle of repose of 33°. The limiting height to diameter ratio of the bin is __________.
solution:
• The limiting height-to-diameter ratio separating “shallow-bin” from “deep-bin” lateral-pressure behaviour is derived from Rankine’s passive earth-pressure relation applied to the grain mass, giving the classical result (H/D)limit = tan(45° + φ/2), where φ is the angle of repose (used here as a surrogate for the internal friction angle).
• With φ = 33°: (H/D)limit = tan(45° + 16.5°) = tan(61.5°) ≈ 1.84, inside the accepted range 1.83–1.85.

subtopic: “…godowns, bins and grain silos, packaging material and machines.”
question: A cylindrical silo, 3 m in diameter and 20 m high, is filled with barley having bulk density of 625 kg m⁻³. Coefficient of friction between grain and the bin wall is 0.45 and the ratio of lateral pressure to vertical pressure is 0.4. The lateral pressure at the base of the bin in kPa will be __________.
solution:
• Janssen’s equation for vertical pressure at depth h in a silo: σv = (γR)/(μk) × [1 – exp(–μkh/R)], where R = hydraulic radius = D/4 (for a circular silo), γ = unit weight of grain, μ = wall friction coefficient, k = lateral/vertical pressure ratio.
• γ = 625 × 9.81 = 6131.25 N/m³. R = 3/4 = 0.75 m. μk = 0.45×0.4 = 0.18.
• μkh/R = 0.18×20/0.75 = 4.8. exp(–4.8) ≈ 0.00823.
• σv = (6131.25×0.75/0.18)×(1–0.00823) = 25,546.9 × 0.99177 ≈ 25,336.8 Pa.
• Lateral pressure = k × σv = 0.4 × 25,336.8 ≈ 10,135 Pa ≈ 10.13 kPa, inside the accepted range 10.1–10.2.
Section 7 — Dairy and Food Engineering

subtopic: human, animal, mechanical, electrical, wind, solar and biomass
question: A solar photovoltaic system comprising solar photovoltaic array, inverter and a motor-pump unit is installed for supplying drinking water in a village. There are 24 modules in the array and each module contains 36 number of cells of size 104×104 mm with a conversion efficiency of 12.8%. The global solar radiation incident normally on the cells is 945 W m⁻². The power consumed in lifting the water is found to be 435 W. If the pump-motor unit efficiency is 45%, the efficiency of the inverter is
solution: Total cell area = 24 modules × 36 cells × (0.104×0.104 m²) = 864 × 0.010816 = 9.345 m². Array (DC) power output = Area × Irradiance × cell efficiency = 9.345 × 945 × 0.128 = 1130.4 W. Electrical power needed at motor input = hydraulic (lifting) power / pump-motor efficiency = 435/0.45 = 966.7 W. Inverter efficiency = (power delivered to motor)/(array DC power) = 966.7/1130.4 = 85.52%.

question:
Fish fillets at −1 °C are being frozen in Individual Quick Freezing (IQF) system using air at −40 °C. The product has a characteristic dimension of 10 cm with a density of 1200 kg·m⁻³. Thermal conductivity of the product is 2.5 W·m⁻²·K⁻¹, the convective heat transfer coefficient is 100 W·m⁻²·K⁻¹ and the latent heat of fusion is 300 kJ·kg⁻¹. If the fillet is considered as an infinite plate, the freezing time, in minutes, is __________. (Rounded off to 2 decimal places)
-type split: MCQ — 31 questions; MSQ — 4 questions (Q.21–Q.24); NAT — 30 questions.
Soil and Water Conservation Engineering was the single heaviest subject section at 16 marks, spread widely across Hydrology (3), Soil & Water Erosion (3), Fluid Mechanics, Soil Mechanics and Surveying.
Farm Power and Engineering Mathematics tied at 13 marks each. Within Farm Power, Tractors and Power Tillers alone contributed 5 questions — with human engineering and safety appearing twice (Q.27 percentile design rule, Q.52 vibration decibels), an area candidates often neglect.
Irrigation and Drainage Engineering was unusually light this year at 9 marks, in contrast to its heavier weight in other sessions.
The paper contained a block of four MSQ questions (Q.21–Q.24), all 1 mark, all conceptual. MSQs carry no negative marking but require every correct option to be selected — partial selection earns nothing.
Several questions rewarded recognising a convention or definition rather than heavy computation: Q.27 (95ᵗʰ percentile for clearance dimensions), Q.29 (bite length depends only on the speed ratio, so the answer is zero), Q.20 (k/h for a cylinder versus 2k/h for a sphere) and Q.31 (the USLE exponent m = 0.5 for slopes ≥ 5 %).
Two questions warrant caution. Q.64 is convention-dependent — the official range is reproduced only by one of the two textbook pairings for representative particle size (see the note in that solution). Q.65 was cancelled with marks awarded to all, its thermal conductivity having been printed with heat-transfer-coefficient units.
solution:
Plank’s equation for freezing time is:
t = (ρ L_f)/(T_f − T_a) × [P a/h + R a²/k]
For an infinite plate (slab): P = 1/2 and R = 1/8, with a = the full thickness.
Step 1 — substitute the data:
ρ = 1200 kg·m⁻³ ; L_f = 300 kJ·kg⁻¹ = 300,000 J·kg⁻¹
T_f − T_a = −1 − (−40) = 39 °C
a = 0.10 m ; h = 100 W·m⁻²·K⁻¹ ; k = 2.5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹
Step 2 — the two shape terms:
P a/h = (0.5 × 0.10)/100 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴
R a²/k = (0.125 × 0.01)/2.5 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴
Sum = 1.0 × 10⁻³
Step 3 — freezing time:
t = (1200 × 300,000/39) × 1.0 × 10⁻³
= 9,230,769 × 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 9230.8 s
Step 4 — convert to minutes:
t = 9230.8/60 = 153.85 minutes
Why the key is MTA. The question was cancelled and marks awarded to all candidates. The source of the ambiguity is visible in the question itself: the thermal conductivity is stated with the units W·m⁻²·K⁻¹, which are the units of a heat transfer coefficient, not of a thermal conductivity (W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹). There is also genuine ambiguity over whether the “characteristic dimension” of 10 cm is the full slab thickness a (as assumed above) or the half-thickness, which would change the answer substantially. The value above is the standard interpretation.
